summary: Sense 1: revise the gloss
after: Fieber bekommen; to burn (intr) (figuratively); (von Wetter/Hitze) heiß werden, brennen
rationale: Add the omitted literal weather/heat meaning already implied by inherited ḥayəm u=yawmo and independently attested with the cognate subject u ḥemo. Preserve the inherited fever and figurative wording.

summary: The aspect contrast is supported morphologically: ḥayəm/ḥayəmno in Preterit Intransitive, kḥayəm in ko-Preterit, ḥoyəm/contracted ḥōm in Infectum. The first-person fever report can describe a current result of becoming feverish.
Literal ambient heating was already present in the inherited hot-day idiom but absent from the numbered gloss. No new root, stem, or Detransitive use is introduced.
The reader’s PrS 52/86 context includes the next clause outside the supplied verse; the added example uses only the assigned verse and its corresponding edition fragment.
Jan Beṯ-Şawoce: the supplied English is project machine translation. All semantic decisions rest on the Turoyo; English quotations are retained verbatim and are not edition translations.
The single -wo predicate is provisionally Infectum-wa in a habitual account of multiple patients. Its a-vocalism is retained as supplied, without reconstructing a new base form.
The ending əzzənwo and lifetime formula concern the subsequent deaths, not the lexical meaning of ḥaymiwo. The fever predicate and death clause remain distinct.
Round 1 already broadens the numbered gloss to literal ambient heat. No duplicate gloss change, sense or hot-day idiom is proposed.
Confirm whether ḥayəmto at 84/32 is a productive Part act. or an independent adjective; its -to differs from the feminine ḥayimo fever predicate.
The inherited HD 85 injury quotation matches MAC Hanna Dewo/114 in this corpus. Confirm the relation between the legacy numbering and current verse scheme before replacing the citation.
MAC Hanna Dewo/114 contains two repeated koḥōm tokens but only one supplied occurrence record. The output covers the eight supplied records exactly and does not invent a ninth.
Confirm ḥaymiwo in Jan 2.33/5414 as Infectum-wa rather than Preterit-wa; the habitual account favours it, but the a-vowel itself does not settle the box.
Ambient heat with cognate ḥemo contrasts with fever whose subject can be the ill person or feminine ḥəmto. These are subject-coding patterns, not evidence for an unexpressed object case.
The sun is described by predicative ḥayəmto at 84/32. Its relation to a verbal Part act. remains unresolved; the literal hot meaning is secure.
Jan adds recurrent fever in typhus patients with a one-to-three-day duration. This supports the inherited fever meaning; it does not make ḥym itself a typhus or death verb.
